summary:
Firebreak is a web dashboard that analyzes, summarizes, ranks, then visualizes 26 NASA space-station fire investigations into an interactive 3-D simulation viewer.

Fire behaves differently in space than it does on earth. NASA has run fire experiments, and the results sit in the PSI archive and in hundreds of reports—making them hard to search and compare due to variances.

Future crews will live in different air than the station. The station uses normal sea-level air (21% oxygen at 101.3 kPa), while NASA's planned Moon base and pressurized rover use 30% oxygen at 70.3 kPa. More oxygen makes things burn more easily.

Firebreak lets you pick a habitat and see which of 26 NASA fire investigations apply—with a plain-language summary and every claim linked to its source. An SI assistant operates on only NASA papers and data, and refuses when the records do not cover the question.
details:
1. Project Details

1.1 The problem

Fire behaves strangely in space. NASA has studied and experimented on it for decades, but the experiment results sit in separate records on NASA’s database, each in its own format. A researcher designing habitats who asks “which experiment results apply to the air in my habitat?” has no tool that answers that question. For example, the NASA Technical reports Server (NTRS), NASA’s paper search engine, matches by keyword only. The PSI archive is organized one experiment at a time, meaning comparing data across experiments with different formats is difficult. General chatbots hallucinate answers, and don’t show proper sources.

This question is becoming increasingly urgent as NASA gears for its Artemis program, the missions returning people to the moon. They plan long stays in habitats with more oxygen than the ISS in space right now, which makes things burn more easily. The future crews need answers matched to their specific environment. Firebreak gives them the answers, and traces every claim to NASA’s own records.

1.2 What it does

What it does. Firstly, you pick where your crew will live among three locations: the International Space Station (21% oxygen, 101.3 kPa), a Moon base (30% oxygen, 70.3 kPa), or a pressurized rover. Upon picking a location, the whole page then switches to that habitat’s environment data—including oxygen and pressure.

Three things then follow, based on the project guidelines:

Summarizing. The dashboard briefs the user by giving them short takeaways for the habitat, relating to safety, how the fire behaves, how the environment may interact with it, and so on. Each brief links back to its source information.

Ranking. We rank all 26 NASA PSI combustion investigations by fit to your habitat, using five checks: oxygen match and pressure match (both count double), how directly it studies fire safety, whether it flew in space, and how well its stated goal fits. An experiment whose tested range includes your habitat scores full marks, and the score falls in a straight line the further you are outside it. A check the record cannot answer counts as half. The rule is printed on the site word for word. Filter by Prevention (stopping fires before they start), Detection (noticing fires early) or Suppression (putting fires out).

Interpretation (Ask SI). You can also ask a question about the habitat or the fire’s behavior in plain English. Each answer goes through four steps: it searches our 64 public sources, reranks the passages by meaning, then uses the relevant passages to source its writing. After that, it checks every claim again. A claim whose quote is missing from the source, or does not support it, is dropped from the answer. The answer shows every source sentence. If the records do not cover the question, it says so instead of guessing.

We also opted to go further than the given requirements, and our dashboard also contains these features:

Compare. Side-by-side comparisons of experiment data, including experiment conditions, fuel, and what was measured.

Team models (Predictive SI). You can edit the oxygen and pressure sliders to see the predicted response flame size, burning rate, and the chance a droplet breaks apart. Each prediction shows its tested range. Outside it, the site greys out the flame-size number and says it is not valid there, and labels the other predictions "outside tested ranges". To see how the models are built and tested: see section 4.3.

What to test next (Gaps in data). It shows where NASA has no data yet for future habitats.

A large feature we opted to add that was not in the challenge statement was the Visualization and Playback portion.

See it.

Replay. A 3D scene of a NASA Saffire fire test, then the same flame under your habitat's conditions. It is built from real experiment numbers.

Evidence Drawer. Click any experiment in the library panel on the side to see its data: conditions, measurements, related experiments, and download its data.

On Earth. Ways the research already helps people, from water-mist extinguishers to better smoke detectors.Figure 1. The one-screen console on Moon Base, with the library panel, 3D fire scene and Ask SI panel.

1.2b A worked example: one engineer, one question

Mara is a safety engineer designing a Moon-base module.

Pick. Mara picks Moon Base as their location. The page loads the 3-D scene and the environment variables: 30% oxygen at 70.3 kPa, compared to the International Space Station default of 21% at 101.3 kPa.

Rank. The experiments more relevant to the moon base rankings show up at the top of the list. One is the ACME CFI-G (PSI-159), burning flames at up to 85% oxygen at microgravity. The top three are now FLEX (PSI-69), FLEX-2 (PSI-68), and ACME CFI-G (PSI-159). Mara can now explore the papers most relevant to their research case.

Ask. Mara drags the research into the Ask SI chat panel and asks, “Based on the top ranking papers, which are the greatest fire risks to a moon base that I should prepare for?” The SI’s answer searches the records for the relevant papers, then cites the FLEX and FLEX-2 papers, where each claim prints its source. 

Below is a sample of the question-and-answer from the Ask SI feature:

Sample:

Question: “Based on the top ranking papers, which are the greatest fire risks to a moon base that I should prepare for?”

SI Answer: “The evidence names two fire risks: lithium ion batteries, used in electronics and space suits, and the not-yet-chosen fabric for future lunar crew clothing. The evidence does not test a 30% oxygen, 70.3 kPa Moon base air, so it cannot say how either risk would change there. It does not cover partial gravity either, so nothing here shows how the Moon's gravity would affect these fires.”

Predict. In the Team models tab, Mara sets oxygen to the Moon-base level. The flame-size number turns grey with the warning "not valid here", because the model never saw air like this. The burning rate (0.73 mm²/s) still shows, labelled "outside tested ranges": an extrapolation, not a measurement.

Plan. Now Mara knows there’s a gap in the research for partial-gravity data, and will ask NASA for this experiment in the future.

Figure 2. Rank step. NASA fire experiments ranked by fit to the Moon base, with scores.

Figure 3. Ask step. Ask SI answers using only the selected sources.

1.3 How it works

CATBOOST MODEL

1. THE JOB

CatBoost predicts one thing on the site: the droplet diameter at which the flame goes out (d_ext, in mm), learned from NASA FLEX runs on the ISS.

• Training set: 196 runs that recorded a flame-out size, spread over 71 test days.

• Inputs (7): fuel, pressure p, mole fractions of O₂, N₂, CO₂ and He, and the starting diameter d₀.

• Physics features, computed from the inputs only, never from results:

  – O₂ partial pressure: p_O₂ = X_O₂ · p

  – Mixture heat capacity: c_p,mix = Σₖ Xₖ · c_p,ₖ

  – Mixture conductivity: k_mix = Σₖ Xₖ · kₖ

  – A flame-temperature proxy: X_O₂ / c_p,mix

  – The droplet size squared: d₀²

2. GRADIENT BOOSTING: THE CORE IDEA

The model is a sum of many small trees, each one correcting what the trees before it got wrong:

   F_M(x) = F₀ + η · Σₘ₌₁ᴹ hₘ(x)

• F₀ is the starting guess: the mean flame-out size.

• hₘ is tree number m. We use M = 300 trees.

• η is the learning rate, 0.05. Each tree's correction is shrunk to 5%, so no single tree dominates.

Each round:

1. Compute the residual of every run: rᵢ = yᵢ − Fₘ₋₁(xᵢ). For squared-error loss L = ½(y − F)², the residual is exactly the negative gradient −∂L/∂F, hence the name "gradient" boosting.

2. Fit a small tree hₘ that predicts those residuals.

3. Add η · hₘ to the model and repeat.

3. THE TREES THEMSELVES

• Symmetric (oblivious) trees: every node on a level asks the same question (same feature, same threshold). With depth 4 there are exactly 4 questions and 2⁴ = 16 leaves. A run's leaf is just its 4 yes/no answers read as a binary number:

    leaf = Σₖ₌₀³ 2ᵏ · 𝟙[x_fₖ > tₖ]

  This makes the trees fast, very regular and hard to overfit, which matters with only 196 rows.

• Choosing splits: each feature is first binned into at most 254 thresholds. For each level, CatBoost tries the candidate (feature, threshold) pairs and keeps the one that cuts the squared error of the residuals the most.

• Leaf values with L2 regularisation (λ = 5): each leaf's value is its average residual, pulled toward zero:

    wⱼ = ( Σᵢ∈leaf j rᵢ ) / ( nⱼ + λ )

  A leaf holding only a few runs therefore can't take an extreme value.

• Ordered boosting is CatBoost's signature technique. It computes each run's residual from a model built only on runs that come before it in a random ordering, so the model never scores itself on data it has already fitted. This removes the "prediction shift" bias that ordinary boosting suffers on small datasets.

4. ONE RULE WE ADDED: A MONOTONE CONSTRAINT

Physically, a bigger droplet should never go out at a smaller size. We forced the model to respect that:

  d₀ₐ ≤ d₀ᵦ  ⇒  F(…, d₀ₐ) ≤ F(…, d₀ᵦ)

CatBoost enforces this by rejecting any split whose leaf values would break the ordering. It's version 2 of the model; the original had no such rule.

Settings: 300 trees, depth 4, η = 0.05, λ = 5, seed 0. No tuning on test data. A nested search reached 0.484 mm against 0.487 mm with the fixed settings, so we kept the fixed ones.

5. HOW WE TESTED IT

Repeated grouped K-fold: fires from the same test day share hardware and conditions, so a whole day is always held out together.

• Split the test days into 5 groups, train on 4, predict the hidden one. Repeat this 10 times with new random splits, giving 50 test folds.

• Score each fold with RMSE = √( (1/n) Σᵢ (ŷᵢ − yᵢ)² ).

Results (RMSE in mm, mean ± spread over the 50 folds):

• Guess the mean:                      1.037 ± 0.124

• Ridge (linear):                      0.566 ± 0.068

• CatBoost v1:                         0.497 ± 0.067 (beat Ridge in 86% of folds)

• CatBoost v2 (physics + monotone):    0.487 ± 0.059

• Leakage check: an ordinary random split, which lets runs from the same day sit in both training and test, scored 0.452. That's only slightly better than the strict 0.497, so same-day leakage is small.

• What drives the prediction: we shuffled one input at a time on held-out days and measured how much the error grew:

  – d₀: +0.667 mm

  – O₂: +0.313 mm

  – fuel: +0.160 mm

  – pressure: ≈ 0

• Uncertainty band: q is the 90th percentile of |y − ŷ| from grouped testing on the training days:

    band = ŷ ± q,  q = 0.84 mm

  On held-out days this band covered 92% of real runs. That's the "likely between" range shown on the card.

6. THE TWO MODELS BESIDE IT

CatBoost had to beat a simpler model for each job, and it lost twice:

• Burning rate K: Ridge regression won, with RMSE 0.074 mm²/s; CatBoost was worse in 90% of folds because the relationship is close to linear. Ridge minimises:

    Σᵢ (yᵢ − xᵢᵀβ)² + α‖β‖²,  α = 1

• Chance the droplet breaks apart: a calibrated logistic model won:

    P = 1 / (1 + e^−(β₀ + βᵀx))

  It scored AUC 0.857 and Brier score 0.114, and its average predicted chance matched the real rate to within 0.1 points.

7. HOW THE SITE USES ALL THREE

None of the models run in the browser. Each was evaluated once on a grid of every setting, and the What-if tool looks the answers up. The burn animation then follows the textbook d²-law:

  d(t)² = d₀² − K·t

  flame-out time: t_ext = (d₀² − d_ext²) / K

Two textbook formulas appear next to the data as labelled theory, never as data:

• Burning rate: K = (8k / ρ_l c_p) · ln(1 + B). It moves in the same direction as our model in 100% of the oxygen, helium and CO₂ cases. Real FLEX droplets burned at about 67% (methanol) and 35% (heptane) of this value.

• Gravity effect (Ranz–Marshall correlation):

    K_g / K₀ = 1 + 0.3 · Gr^¼ · Pr^⅓,  Gr = g · (ΔT/T) · d³ / ν²

  For a 2 mm droplet in air this gives about 1.33× on the Moon, 1.41× on Mars and 1.52× on Earth.

8. WHERE IT STOPS

Moon Base air (30% O₂, 527 mmHg) sits at the edge of the FLEX data. Most runs there broke apart, so only 9 recorded a flame-out size. That's why the site crosses out the flame-out prediction for that air instead of showing a number it can't stand behind.

Finally, here is a graph that illustrates how it learns:

Figure 4. Graph of the CatBoost Model learning process.

1.4 How we tested it

We tested the Ask SI box on 100 questions, 23 of them held back so we never tuned on them. It refused all 19 off-topic questions, answered all 10 data and 10 model questions correctly, and none of the 133 claims it quoted failed the second check that each quote really supports its claim. Testing also showed it often cited general NASA overview pages instead of the actual research reports, so we made it prefer the reports. That raised the share of research answers citing the right paper from 58% to 65%. We tested the prediction models only on ISS test days they never saw during training, repeated 50 times, and each had to beat a simpler model to be used. That test showed a plain straight-line model predicts burning rate better than CatBoost, so the site uses the simpler model for that number.

Here is a graph that illustrates how we tested it:

Figure 5. Graph of how the model was tested.

HOW ASK SI WORKS (RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION)

1. THE JOB. Ask SI answers questions using only our library of 90 NASA sources, split into 558 passages. It never answers from general knowledge.

• The SI is Claude Haiku, used in three separate roles: re-ranking passages, writing claims, and checking claims.

• Plain code does everything that can be checked exactly: search, gates, quote matching.

2. DATA FACTS FIRST. Before any paper is searched, the question is matched against facts computed from NASA tables (e.g. "fabrics were tested at 16.4 to 21% O₂").

• Each fact is scored with a BM25-style weighting:

    s = Σ_w idf(w) · c·2.2 / ( c + 1.2·(0.25 + 0.75·dl/avg) )

 Where c is how often word w appears in the fact and dl/avg is the fact's length relative to the average.

• Coverage gate: the share of the question's words found in the fact must be ≥ 0.5. If the question contains no fire-science word at all, every word must match (so "What is dark matter?" matches nothing).

• Up to 2 facts are kept. They are shown first, labelled "computed from the tables, not written by SI".

3. KEYWORD SEARCH (code, BM25).

• Tokenise: lowercase, split on non-letters, drop stop words ("the", "of", "how" …). Add known synonyms (query expansion) and the matched fact's keywords.

• Rarity of each word over all N passages:

    idf(t) = ln( 1 + (N − dₜ + 0.5) / (dₜ + 0.5) ),  dₜ = passages containing t

• Score of passage P for query Q:

    BM25(P,Q) = Σ_{t∈Q} idf(t) · f(t,P)·(k₁+1) / ( f(t,P) + k₁·(1 − b + b·|P|/avgLen) )

  with k₁ = 1.5 (how fast repeats stop adding score) and b = 0.75 (penalty for long passages).

• Overview weight: general NASA summary pages are scored × 0.75, so real research reports win ties. This raised "right paper in the top 5" from 25 to 28 of 34 tuning questions, and from 18 to 20 of 23 held-out ones.

• Per-source cap: at most 2 passages per source, so one long paper can't fill the list. The top 20 form the pool.

4.OFF-TOPIC GATE (code). For the top 5 passages, it computes the rarity-weighted share of the question's words they contain:

    coverage = max_P  Σ_{t∈Q∩P} idf(t) / Σ_{t∈Q} idf(t)

If coverage < 0.3, there are no matching data facts, and the question has no fire-science word, Ask SI answers "the records don't cover that" and stops. No SI is called.

5. RE-RANK (SI). The SI reads the 20 passages (each marked kind = "report" or "overview") and returns JSON: the passages that actually answer the question, best first, or "none relevant".

• Rules it gets: judge only from the passage text, not from outside knowledge; prefer results over plans; prefer a report over an overview when equal.

• Code validates the reply: invented or repeated passage numbers are ignored, and an unusable reply keeps the keyword order.

• Measured on 83 labelled questions: the right source came first in 58 (49 with keywords alone); it said "none relevant" for 20 of 20 off-topic questions and 0 of 83 real ones.

6. WRITE CLAIMS (SI). The top passages, at most 6 sources, are passed in. The SI must return JSON claims, each one short sentence plus one exact quoted sentence from its source.

• Passages are wrapped as data, so instructions inside a paper can't steer the SI.

• For papers NASA marks "short quotes only", it may not copy more than 15 consecutive words.

7. QUOTE CHECK (code). Each quote is normalised (Unicode NFKC, spacing, quote marks) and must appear in its source passage word for word, on word boundaries:

    keep(claim) ⇔ normalise(quote) ⊂ normalise(source passage)

Claims that cite a source not given, have no quote, or copy too much from a short-quote paper are dropped.

8. SUPPORT CHECK (SI, second pass). A separate SI call reads each claim next to its quote and answers "supported" or "not supported".

• Not supported → dropped.

• No clear verdict → kept but flagged "not double-checked".

In our test, 0 of 133 claims failed this check.

9. SUMMARY (SI). A short answer is written only from the claims that survived, and code checks it adds no new numbers or sources. Short-quote papers show at most 15 words on screen; the full check ran on the complete sentence.

10. WHEN SOMETHING FAILS.

• One automatic retry for timeouts, rate limits (429), server errors (5xx), unreadable replies, or all claims being dropped.

• If it still fails, Ask SI falls back to showing the best matching quotes with no SI-written answer, and says why. This happened on 1 of 100 test questions.

• Demo questions have saved answers, so they load instantly; new questions run live (median 7.4 s).

11. HOW WE TESTED IT. 100 questions: 57 research, 19 off-topic, 10 data, 10 model, 2 with no data, 2 others. 23 of the research questions were held back and never used for tuning.

• Off-topic refused: 19 / 19

• Data facts correct: 10 / 10;  model facts correct: 10 / 10

• Cited the exact paper we labelled as correct: 37 / 57 (65%); held-out: 15 / 23

• Claims failing the support check: 0 / 133

• A larger SI reviewer (Claude Sonnet) judged the 57 research answers: 21 fully answered, 26 partly, 10 not.

12. WHERE IT STOPS. It knows only the 90 sources. Keyword search can miss a question worded very differently from the papers. Strict checks drop doubtful claims, so some answerable questions come back partial or unanswered. That's the trade we chose: precision over completeness.

Figure 6. Graph of Ask SI process.

1.5 Limits 

DATA. Team models learned only from methanol and heptane droplets (274 FLEX runs). No other fuels or solids are predicted.

• The solid-material map covers one fabric and 23 tests, all at ≤21% O₂. Moon Base air (30%) is untested for solids.

• No PSI experiment ran in Moon or Mars gravity. Those numbers are labelled textbook estimates.

TEAM MODELS. Moon Base air sits at the edge of the FLEX data, with only 9 flame-out sizes recorded near it. That prediction is crossed out there, and the break-up chance is shown as a trend.

• Predictions exist only for a fixed grid of settings, as research estimates, not safety values.

ASK SI: A SCOPE, NOT JUST A LIMIT. Ask SI answers only from our library of 90 NASA sources, never from general knowledge.

• Every claim quotes an exact sentence. Code verifies the quote exists, and a second SI pass checks it supports the claim: 0 of 133 failed.

• It refuses what the library doesn't cover (19 of 19 off-topic questions).

• The trade-off is precision over completeness: some answerable questions go unanswered. It cited the exact right paper in 65% of research answers.

• Keyword search can miss differently worded questions.

IN ONE LINE. Firebreak says only what NASA's records support, labels every estimate, and leaves a question open rather than guess. Asking it something unrelated warrants a response: "This is not in the records".

1.6 Why it matters

In 1967, Apollo 1’s flash fire prevented it from ever leaving the earth; in 1997, one of  the Mir space station’s oxygen generators ignited instead of releasing oxygen steadily. Fire is one of the most dangerous emergencies in space—nobody truly expects it. It brings with it both disaster and lessons.

The future Moon habitats may need to run richer oxygen with lower pressure to sustain human life itself. This is the problem—at higher oxygen concentrations, flammability becomes more prevalent; material ignition gets easier and flames spread faster. 

Habitat and safety engineers need to account and optimize for this, researchers need it to devise safer configurations, and the crew that will live inside it needs it the most. On Earth, we already have smoke detectors, water-mist extinguishers, and firefighter gear. Thus, we tested 3 different habitats at lunar conditions with the goal of applying current research data into designing possible habitats for future lunar settlement.

1.7 What makes it different 

Firebreak is more than a chatbot placed on top of the database. Weak spots are inevitable in our app but we are able to cover those. The SI can overstate one thing but a claim checker will be available and the SI handles only one of the five checks. Since rule-based rankings cannot read the nuance of the text, the SI will clarify the ranking in words. Furthermore, our models are only trained on 274 FLEX runs—outside of the tested range, error bands and a warning, if it is a guess, is shown. The 3D models only highlight what was measured. For further information, the SI explains why it happened and what could happen next. 

However, the most important part of this project is that it communicates information and data from 90 papers and makes it accessible through the use of visual storytelling. This project does not only aim to reach researchers and professionals, but also students who are curious about the subject. It is a form of communication that brings the problem of fire safety to the spotlight and emphasizes its importance in space missions.

1.8 What's next

As soon as NASA’s experiments LUCI and FM2 report back, we will add gravity results. Additionally, engineers will be able to enter the air of their habitat. Doing so will have the predictions match the properties. Lastly, we will let the library extend to more NASA resorts from future experiments.

2. Use of Super Intelligence

Figure 7. Graph of SI Interactions.

A second pass checks that each quoted sentence supports its claim, and unsupported claims are dropped. TypeSafe (System One model “Jev”) judges how well each experiment’s goal fits the habitat, one of the five ranking checks, and writes fallback answers if Haiku is unavailable. Claude Sonnet 5.5 graded test answers during evaluation only, and is not in the live site. 

SIs utilized are: Claude Haiku 5.5 (Anthropic) writes responses for the “Ask SI” feature using only retrieved NASA passages. A second pass checks if quoted sentences supports its claim, and drops any unsupported claims. TypeSafe (System One model “Jev”) for judges how each experiment’s goal fits the habitat environment through one of five ranking checks while writing fallback answers as if Haiku is unavailable. Claude Sonnet 5.5 graded test answers during evaluation only, and is not used in the live site.

CatBoost, Ridge regression and logistic regression are our own models trained by the team on NASA FLEX data.

SI used to build it
We used Claude Code as a coding assistant, using Anthropic models including Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.2. It helped write and review code for the website (React and Three.js), the server (Hono on Cloudflare Workers), and the Python data pipeline, under our direction. 

The idea and its logic came from the team: Daniel proposed the “relive the fire, then apply it to future missions with habitat-first ranking” while Raenn proposed the keyword-and-meaning search context retrieval. 

We made the design and data choices, ran the tests and wrote the text on the project description. We also reviewed all SI output.

Safeguards
All “Ask SI” Answers cite NASA sources, and off-topic questions are refused. 

We used no SI-generated images of NASA people, logos or missions. 

The habitat pictures are SI-generated and marked “SI-generated image”.
